title: Clinical Mastery: Macular Scarring (Unilateral vs. Bilateral)
summary: Macular scarring represents the terminal phase of various chorioretinal pathologies. Distinguishing between unilateral etiologies (often traumatic or infectious) and bilateral causes (often dystrophic or systemic) is the cornerstone of clinical workup.

Bilateral: AMD (Geographic Atrophy), Stargardt Disease, Best Disease, Pattern Dystrophies, Congenital Infections

rows: Concentric to optic nerve, sub-RPE hemorrhage

sections.title: Red Flags for Active Progression
content: Presence of subretinal fluid (SRF) indicating active CNVM
New lipid exudation at scar margins
Vitritis or anterior chamber cell (Active Infection)

sections.title: Diagnostic Workup Protocol
content: Step 1: Multimodal Imaging (FAF for metabolic health, OCT for structural atrophy)
Step 2: OCT-Angiography to rule out subclinical flow in occult CNVM
Step 3: Serology (IgG/IgM for Toxo, Histoplasma, Syphilis)
Step 4: ERG/EOG if bilateral symmetric dystrophy is suspected

content.explanation: B-Best Disease (Vitelliform), A-AMD (Atrophy), R-Retinitis Pigmentosa (Macular involvement), S-Stargardt (ABCA4 mutation).

sections.title: Clinical Pearls
content: In unilateral scars, always examine the fellow eye periphery for 'satellite' lesions.
FAF is the gold standard for defining the borders of Geographic Atrophy.
Traumatic ruptures often have a latent period for CNVM development; watch 3-6 months post-injury.
Genetic testing is now standard-of-care for idiopathic bilateral maculopathy.
